utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We are, I believe, ready for the next witness, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, the next witness is Dr. Eric Baccard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I would like to introduce a new face on the Prosecution team, one of our new Legal Officers, Ms. Paige Petersen, who is sitting right behind me, and she will be appearing before Your Honours later on in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We look forward to her continued assistance. While we are waiting, I will mention that in June Defence counsel moved to have admitted a document through Witness Richard Ciaglinski. The Prosecution -- that was accepted, but the Prosecution subsequently objected that the document should not have been admitted as Exhibit D165. The Chamber indicated it would give its decision at a later stage. We have considered it. In our view, the document is sufficiently relevant to be admissible. It is true the witness was not able personally to speak in verification of the document, and that is a matter which the Chamber will take into account in assessing its weight; but the document having been admitted without objection, it will remain admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. I believe Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you start out by stating your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: My name is Eric Baccard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is your profession, Mr. Baccard?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I am a forensic pathologist, and I am currently in charge of the scientific unit at the International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And as a forensic pathologist, what is your area of specialisation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As regards forensic medicine, I am specialised in forensic medicine of the living and also specialised in the examination of dead bodies. In particular, as it is indicated in my specialisation in France, I examine bodily injury of the living and also I carry out autopsies of cadavers. I am also a specialist in ballistic wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before working for the International Criminal Court, were you employed by this Tribunal, by the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Madam Prosecutor. I worked on a contract basis for a determined period of time as a forensic doctor in 1989 [as interpreted] in Bosnia and then in Croatia, and then as a forensic pathologist in chief for the ICTY in Kosovo in the year 2000, and from 2001 until 2003 as a forensic consultation for the OTP of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned that you work as a forensic pathologist in chief for the ICTY in Kosovo. Could you give us a bit more information about the nature of your work there.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. My job consisted in -- at the beginning of the year 2000 of setting up the infrastructure and procedures. I participated in the choice of equipment for the morgue which was set up in Orahovac, which is a few kilometres from a particular place, and indeed this infrastructure was composed of a number of specialists in various disciplines who worked within this morgue. To give you an example, at one point in time I had up to ten forensic specialists, but there were also anthropologists, odontologists, X-ray specialists, photographers, and crime scene officers all working under my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And as part of the task of supervising this team that you've referred to, did you also review reports prepared by different international forensic teams during your stay in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, not during my stay in Kosovo, but after that, in other words starting at the end of the year 2000 and then in 2001 until 2002, until the Slobodan Milosevic trial began. Indeed, the OTP asked me to re-examine, in terms of the methodology, the materials used and the methods and the results, to re-examine as I was saying the expertise carried out by numerous international teams who had intervened during the year 1989 in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And as a result of this review that you conducted of the expertise carried out by numerous international teams in 1999 in Kosovo, did you prepare a report for the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Madam Prosecutor, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We will get to your report in a minute. I just wanted to ask you, have you testified before this Tribunal as an expert witness in other cases?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I testified -- I don't remember what year it was, but it was in the trial against Slobodan Milosevic. I testified for two days and then again three days in 2002 I believe. I also testified in the case Milan Milutinovic, and again in the trial against Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And have you qualified as an expert witness and been allowed to express opinions and testimony before any domestic courts before coming to testify in these proceedings today?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Madam Prosecutor. In my specialty of forensic medicine I have 28 years of experience and I am registered on -- at the Court of Appeals in Grenoble and also in the Court of Appeals, the Cour de cassation, as from the end of the year 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just approximately in how many cases have you testified before these courts you have mentioned as an expert witness, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It's extremely different for me to say that because I don't count precisely the number of times I've testified, but probably several hundreds of times. Each year I carry out 200 to 300 expertise. I don't always testify before a court, but I have testified very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Your updated CV is 65 ter 02784.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to go into more detail about the CV, as the document speaks for itself, but I will seek to tender it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, do you wish to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01138.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, we were speaking earlier about the report that you prepared for the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal in relation to exhumations conducted in Kosovo in 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, Your Honours, for reference 65 ter 01809.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would just like you to very briefly explain to the Court the methodology you used in preparing this report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of the report with me here to refer to. It stayed in the witness waiting-room, but I can describe it briefly. The OTP provided a number of documents to me. There were autopsy reports carried out by various teams of various different national origins. There were photo albums, sometimes accompanied by police reports. And these -- well, I examined these various documents. I examined the qualifications of the experts who had carried out the expertise, whether it was autopsies or anthropological examinations or dental examinations depending on which report or which team. I examined whether or not the methods used were in keeping with internationally accepted standards. And when, for reasons of urgency did not make it possible to implement international standards, it was not possible, well I examined the conclusions to see whether they were scientifically valid, in other words, whether in their conclusions they had not sacrificed the essential elements that are required in such an expert report. I also compared the results of the forensic specialists with the photographs, to see whether there are any discrepancies; and when and if there were discrepancies, I took note of them. And in my report, in the annexes of my report, there is a list of elements where I expressed my opinion, where my opinion differed from that of my expert colleagues. Again, they, however, had had the advantage of examining real cases, that is, examining the bodies, whereas I was only examining documents which give you an indirect presentation of reality in the form of photographs and sometimes videos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the conclusions contained in your report are based on your review and analysis of the forensic reports that you were provided?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify, did you participate in any of the exhumations at the sites that were referred to in these reports that you analysed for the purpose of preparing your own expert report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, no, Madam Prosecutor, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How long did it take you to prepare this expert report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Several months. I do not have the exact duration in mind, but it is included in the report -- but I don't have a copy of the report before me just now and you can find that information in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand from your report that you examined exhumation reports that referred to 11 sites and there was one site that had four sub-sites; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to very briefly look at your conclusions regarding some of these sites. We're not going to go through all of them but just through some so that you can explain the methodology you used when examining the underlying material for each one of these sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have up on the screen 65 ter 01809, and I would like to first look at page 37 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a section of your report. Do you have that before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I'm looking at section 2.5 which refers to Djakovica, Milosh Giliq Street specifically. Now, we see that 2.5.1 lists the supporting documents. These, I understand from your report, would have been the forensic material that you examined in order to reach your conclusions regarding this site. Would that be a correct understanding of what is listed there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now if we could go to page 39 under the heading "Conclusion," and in the B/C/S this is page 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in this paragraph and under this heading "Conclusion," and I'm looking at the second paragraph you say: "For the same reason, it was impossible to determine the cause of death or any injury." I would just like to ask you to comment on that conclusion that you reached with -- regarding this site. And if you could explain why you considered it impossible to establish the cause of death for this site.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. It's easy. This is directly related to the state of conservation of the body remains. They were not in the form of complete bodies but only fragments, and in addition these body parts were severely burned and therefore it was extremely difficult to draw any forensic conclusions from these body parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see the first paragraph refers to a minimum number of 20 individuals found at this site. And it says: "... one of them was male, and the rest female or undetermined ..." And could you explain to the Court, and having regard to your answer just now about the body parts being severely burned, how the team that conducted this examination was able to determine the number of individuals concerned at this site or found at this site.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: During the forensic anthropological examination, we took stock of the various bones and prepared an inventory, and on the basis of that inventory we were able to conclude the minimum number of individuals. Sometimes some bones in the human body are found twice, in particular limbs, that is, arms or legs, and in other cases like the ribs or the vertebras there are many more in each body. And therefore, it's sometimes difficult to describe precisely whether you have a fragment of a radius or a cubitus, which are the bones in the lower arm and whether it's left or right. And therefore anthropologists examine the bones that are found in only one copy in each body, and therefore in this sample of human remains all of the bones corresponded to that criterion. In addition, some bones present significant characteristics, that is, as regards the gender or the age of the individual. If you find those bones in the inventory, you can then determine clearly the age or the gender of the bones or bone fragments; in other cases, the bones could belong to male or female bodies because there's no particular criterion. For the information of the Court, the bones that are particularly significant as regards the sex are the base of the cranium or the pelvic bones, and those bones are particularly useful -- or rather, the bones that are useful to determine the age is the pelvic bone, the pubic bone, or the fourth rib, for example, or the skull bones. These -- if we find such bone fragments, we can draw conclusions as regards the gender of the body. If we don't find those bones, it's much more difficult and that explains the relatively low percentage of discriminating factors in this particular sample.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. We also see that in the conclusion you have noted: "... no blindfold or ligature was noted." Why is it important to -- or why did you find it important to note that in this case, and I note that you have also noted that for other sites. So why is that information contained in the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: On the basis of prior expertise before 1999 when I was in Bosnia or Croatia or in Kosovo in the year 2000, in some places, in some sites and for certain victims, we did find such elements, that is, ligatures, people's hands or ankles were tied or they had blindfolds on their eyes. So that is part of the kind of screening that we carry out when carrying out such a forensic examination in similar circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We'd like to now move to a different site, and this is a site of Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is on page 44 of the English version and page 48, I believe, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I understand, sir, and you have briefly referred to this in an earlier answer that Izbica was an unusual site because you didn't have forensic reports or forensic material regarding the bodies of the victims there. Could you explain a bit what was -- what type of material did you review to reach your conclusions regarding the Izbica site?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I did have forensic reports, but those reports had been developed on the basis of a limited number of body parts, body remains, and therefore these were written reports prepared by Professor Dominique Lecomte and Dr. Walter Vorhauer. I also had the crime scene examination report which was prepared by Officer -- the "Commissaire Divisionnaire" Officer Dominique Gaillardon and his team. And there was also a video and some photographs extracted from that video which was produced by a witness shortly after the events. Therefore, I used those three sources of information in order to carry out this examination of the whole set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to a video and 1.078 photographs extracted from the video. Could you explain how it is that you used those materials to reach your conclusions regarding this site?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Of course, by way of introduction, we need to recall the fact that this video was not shot by a forensic specialist. That was the main obstacle. Indeed we could only see one side of the victims' bodies. In addition, the clothing was not removed so that the bodies were clothed. Sometimes there were blankets over them, and therefore you could only see the face or the hands or body parts that remain visible. The quality of the video itself was insufficient and did not make it possible to enlarge the picture in such a way that it be usable, that is, we couldn't enlarge it more than two or three times. That represents a limit, and I mentioned this clearly in my report. In other words, only some of the images were actually used, that is, where the wounds were clearly visible. The first task was to determine whether or not the video was made up, whether it was not the way the bodies were actually positioned. That conclusion was not probable because there were a number of forensic details that we would never have had if the scene had been made up, if it had been a picture of false victims. So once we determined that aspect, the victims were examined one after the other on the basis of certain photographs. In some photographs the same victims appeared -- there were several victims, and therefore we had to examine them individually so that we not count the same person several times because that same person might have been found on several photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify your answer, when you were saying whether -- you were trying to determine whether or not the video was made up, you said that the conclusion was not probable because there were a number of forensic details that you would have never had if the scene had been made up. Could you explain what it is that -- what you meant by this, which were those forensic details that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, mainly the way in which the body is set after death, for instance, the bodily lividity, the colouring of -- the way in which the blood sets under the pressure of gravity in some position -- some parts of the body, the accumulation of blood in some areas means that the body becomes red or dark red or purple in some places. The way in which the bodily fluids seep out or so either blood or through the nostrils. This is also something you can relate to the position of the body. The pressure points also, the way in which the body was positioned meant that -- means that there were pressure exerted in some specific points. And these are elements that we always review and list during such pathological review.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know why it is that the forensic team that went to this site was unable to examine the bodies, the victims?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: According to the information that had been collected, these bodies had in fact been exhumed before these teams came on site.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, was this method that you used of making your assessments on the basis of a videos or/and photographs an accepted method in your field?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It often occurs that such photographical material is submitted to pathologists for review, when indeed the body is not available or when the body is available but only with a slight delay after the events occurred. In such instances, the judge may request that the expert give an assessment on the basis of photographs or video footage. I've had to do that on a number of occasions indeed in front of -- before French courts. This is something that I also had to do when I served as an expert with the first UN investigation team in Cote d'Ivoire. So it is an accepted practice. We know, of course, for the reasons that I stated previously, that there are limitations to operating in such a way. We know that the best way to conduct an expertise is, of course, by examining the body itself. It is not an expertise as such, as I expressed in this report and in previous reports. What in fact we're doing in such circumstances is expressing an opinion on the basis of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Appendix 5 of your report contains your conclusions regarding the specific site and your assessment on the photographs. And I would like to show you a page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Page 106 if we could have that up on the screen. This is page 117 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just so you can explain to the Court how it is that you examined these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if only the English could be displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to ask you specifically about the language used in your conclusions. We see the first sentence says: "... on the front above the left eye brow, it exists an injury consistent with a gun-shot wound ..." If you could just comment on that and explain with regard to the first photograph we see here how it is you made your assessment as to the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, let me first say that the stills that you see on your screen are not the stills that I myself had to review. The quality of these pictures is much -- was much better than what you see on the screen. The ones I had, even though they were -- there were mistakes and lax in quality was much better. There was the possibility of zooming in and seeing specific details. On each of these pictures, I reviewed the parts of the body that were visible. I examined the wounds, injuries, the blood, whether we were talking about bruises or fluids running out. I looked also at the liver mortis that I mentioned earlier. I looked at the pressure points. I looked at the possible plants that might have -- vegetables that might have grown or been present, and I did not review really anything covered by the clothes, but I did look at the clothes. And there were two things that were interesting on the clothes, i.e., the defects, the ripping of some of the clothes. Some of the tears and rips were specific of the way in which projectiles might have impacted the clothes, and also blood-stains on the clothes. So this does not mean that I could come to absolute conclusions, and that is precisely why in my report I reviewed a number of elements that I felt I could supply the OTP with. On the specific pictures we're talking about here, I was looking at the environment of these bodies, the position they were in, the way the head rested, for instance, the blood-stains, and the way this might have matched blood clots that were visible on some pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you said that based on your analysis you could not come to absolute conclusions. Does that explain why you have used that sort of phrasing in this page we're looking at of "consistent with gun-shot wounds" when you're reaching your conclusions regarding these two bodies?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm saying, Madam, because you must understand that an autopsy, a forensic examination, includes a number of stages. First of all, X-rays, and then the overall examination of the body even before you start proceeding with more detailed examination of the body. Now, my inspection -- that inspection was something I could only do through still photography. There was only one specific angle that I could have for these bodies, and I didn't have the degree of detail and access that forensic pathologists might have had in a morgue. So there was some distance. And I couldn't really come closer to the body, touch the body if I had to. I couldn't dissect the bodies. These were the limitations I was subjected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I would like to now move to a different site and this is a site of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if he we could go to page 78 in the English and this is page 91 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we'll again ask you about -- to comment on your conclusions regarding this site. Now, we see in your conclusions that you refer to two individuals who've been identified, and the last bullet point says: "Causes of death of the four individuals of" a certain exhibit which is mentioned there "cannot be determined." Can you explain why it is that for these four individuals found at this site the cause of death was not established?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I think I need to look at the report for a few moments, if you'll allow me. I can only read one page of the report. Could I maybe get the beginnings of that section.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could go to page 75, 76 I believe is the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You refer to the identification of three individuals and -- but later in your conclusions you state that the cause of death for four of them could not be established.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There were two anthropologists' reports. One written up by Dr. Black and one by Ms. Roberts. And there were discrepancies in the way some of the bodies were identified, and more specifically Exhibit SCG/33/SR, as -- there were discrepancies between the same references in Dr. Black's and Ms. Roberts' reports. They were listing different sets of bones under the same reference. Moreover, there were two different conclusions they were coming to as to the gender of the individual. Secondly, there was also a discrepancy with respect to the presence or not of a left foot and to the height of the individual. I therefore disregarded that specific case, given the lack of certainty relating to that reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could just look at one final site, this is Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would like to go page 38 of the English, and it's page 36 of the B/C/S. I'm sorry, it's the next page in the English, 33. I don't believe we have the correct page in the English. I'm looking for page 33, and I see we have displayed page 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And again, sir, I would just ask you to comment on the conclusions regarding this site, this is Mala Krusa or Krusha e Vogel which refers to four victims. And I'm specifically interested in the last sentence where it says that: "The status of these remains did not permit to determine the cause of death." If you could comment on that.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Could I, Madam, get a view of the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could go to the previous page, please, page 32 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The state in which the bodies were was in fact the reason why I couldn't give an indication of the cause of death. The bodies were in a skeletal state and had also been severely burnt, at least partially burnt. There was, therefore, no way in which we could establish what sort of wounds had they -- these bodies had suffered and what the cause of death was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the report at this stage this is 65 ter 01809, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01139.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not intend to use court time going through all the underlying material for each one of the sites mentioned in the report. I have prepared a list of these documents which I've provided this morning to the Registrar and also to Defence. And I would just like to ask that at a later stage exhibit numbers be assigned to the underlying reports which are -- have been examined by the expert witness in preparation of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And are you preparing a list of these documents to assist the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I've already handed it this morning, it's been prepared, and Defence has a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I studied the evidence admitted in Milosevic and Milutinovic, and I noticed that some of the exhibits were filed inaccurately. In Milutinovic, for instance, we had a pretty clear situation, as we can see from the trial judgement, that the OTP filed evidence related to Velika Krusa, whereas the questions asked of Dr. Baccard were about Mala Krusa. It was established later only. And in view of the fact that something similar can happen with other evidence, I would prefer to go through exhibits one by one and establish things clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will not spend time at the moment on this. Could I suggest that during the break Prosecution and Defence counsel look at the documents which it is proposed by the Prosecution to tender, and Mr. Djordjevic can indicate whether he has a specific concern about the correctness of a particular document or not judging from his consideration of the earlier cases. In the absence of a particular concern, we will receive the documents. But I would like counsel to first discuss them together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will take care of that at the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that you have testified before as an expert witness in several cases. Did you testify in connection to the report that we've been discussing in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Madam, but I cannot remember which specific locations were mentioned in the Milutinovic case. I remember this report --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I may stop you there. I'm sorry, maybe -- my question is very simple. I'm just asking if you have previously testified with regard to this report in the case of Milutinovic et al., just a simple question. I'm not asking about the specific sites.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, in that case the answer is yes. I thought, Madam, that you were asking me whether this or that location, this or that site, had been mentioned in the Milutinovic case. Now that I understand, let me say that, yes, questions were put to me vis-a-vis this report in both Milosevic and Milutinovic cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to review the transcript of your testimony in the Milutinovic et al. case?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, I did -- at least to a certain extent. I seem to remember that the document I had only covered part of my witness -- expert report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed your transcript in that case, if today you were asked the same questions that you were asked in your testimony in that case, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Very probably, yes, at least concerning the pathological events. There's only one answer I could give for these specific pathological circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the Milutinovic transcript into evidence this is 65 ter 05340, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript of evidence will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P01140.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to now move to a different exhibit. This is 65 ter 05009. And just for -- to ease reference of the witness to the document, I would ask that I be allowed to provide the witness with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of this document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this document? Have you had the chance to review it before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, Madam. This is a document that you provided to me as well as Mr. Sultan when we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And very briefly could you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 on the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is a portion of several documents that you gave to me in order for me to read through them dealing with autopsies that were carried out by my colleague, Professor Peter Vanezis regarding 19 victims, I believe, 19 autopsies which were carried out in the morgue in Pristina. Therefore, these documents are an introduction, so to speak, to the autopsy report that was to follow, I believe. You also gave me a binder with photographs dealing with the exhumation of these victims. The photographs were of poor quality. And another binder containing photographs that were much better in quality which were taken during the autopsy of part of those victims. I don't remember whether there were eight or nine amongst the documents you gave me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, and based on your review of this documentation regarding the exhumation carried out regarding these 19 bodies and your analysis of the photographs, could you provide your comments as to whether in your view standards that are internationally accepted when carrying out exhumations were followed in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, in the English we have the wrong copy -- page. I believe I want the next page. It's page 5. My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. As regards the autopsies of the victims, my answer is: Yes, indeed. The opposite would have been astonishing given the qualifications, the university and professional qualifications of Professor Peter Vanezis. I therefore have absolutely no doubt that international standards were implemented fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have referred now twice to Professor Peter Vanezis. Could you tell us just briefly who he is.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Professor Vanezis is a forensic science and medicine professor. I had the pleasure and honour of meeting him in Kosovo in the year 2000. He's renowned in university circles, and if I remember correctly - I must say I'm not totally certain - but I believe he works in Glasgow if I'm not mistaken. But I'm not a hundred per cent certain of that particular fact. But he is in England for sure, and I believe now he has retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on your review of the documentation that was provided to you regarding the site, was Professor Vanezis the person in charge of these exhumations and autopsies?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As regards the autopsies, he signed the first page of each of those reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to have one of these reports up on the screen. This is 65 ter 05005, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, could you explain to us what is this document that we see up on the screen just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: This is the first page of the autopsy report, which includes the summary of findings, the cause of death, and it is signed by the expert forensic pathologist, in particular it is Professor Peter Vanezis. This is the first page of a report which in fact contains several chapters, several portions. This is a printed, typewritten report, which is drafted later on. Initially a handwritten report is prepared by the forensic specialist who carried out the autopsy, and it is the handwritten report which is used to draft the printed, typewritten, final report. In addition to this report there are a number of annexes which include the anthropology and odontology report, but also annexes with X-ray reports. You may also have an inventory of clothing and other evidence that is filed, that is registered at the point in time when the autopsy is carried out. There might also be the exhumation report which is at the very last page of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And before reviewing the autopsy reports for this specific site, have you had the opportunity to see reports in a similar format, using this similar format before?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This is a format which was developed as the various exhumation and autopsy campaigns were organised by the ICTY, in light of the series of autopsies that were carried out in Bosnia and in Croatia in particular. The format was improved each year by the various forensic teams who participated in the exhumation campaigns and autopsies. This is a report format which is particularly clear, that's an advantage, and it can be used over and over again. It is presented in standard form, and it was done this way because the forensic specialists who come from various different countries, various different university backgrounds agreed that it was acceptable. They all agreed to work on the basis of this standard format.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had told us earlier in your testimony that you worked in Kosovo in 2000 -- in the year 2000. Was this also the format that you used during your work there, during the exhumations that you conducted there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the next page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see, sir, in the top part under the section "A. Description of Remains" that there is a reference to a piece of paper with the name of the victim, Shehide Bogujevci, 66 years old. Based on your review of the materials, could you -- do you know how it is that this individual and others who are concerned in this site were identified?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: On the basis of the information that I read in the documents that you provided to me, these individuals were buried by their family members and the tombs were marked, and therefore the identification had already been carried out. Therefore, these pieces of paper which contained the identification could be seen on the general photographs as well as on the body-bag. There were two cases that you'll perhaps mention in a moment. There was -- there were two identification tags that had been mixed up for two victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We will get to that in a moment. I would like to now scroll down on this same page and zoom in on the section "E. Injuries." We see there's a heading "Findings on fluoroscopy" and a reference to different metallic fragments. If you could explain that information contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. The fluoroscopic and/or X-ray examination, and sometimes you just carry out an X-ray -- or rather, you carry out a fluoroscopy or an X-ray which enables you to examine an image on a screen. You know, you have an X-ray that is run over the body. This test which is used under international standards has several purposes. The first purpose, of course, as is stated here is to identify the precise location in the anatomy where a particular element is found which could explain the cause of death, for example, a bullet, a projectile fragment, a piece of shrapnel. Even before you open the body-bag you can determine that, for example, in the right shoulder there is a projectile. The forensic specialist can therefore concentrate on that particular part of the anatomy. That's the first goal. The second goal is to point out any element that may make it possible to identify the body. For example, if you have ante mortem information whereby the victim had had a fracture of the tibia previously and if they had undergone osteosynthesis, well, the very fact of finding the traces of osteosynthesis on the X-ray will be a very positive element enabling us to confirm the diagnosis or any other prosthesis, for example, of the hip. These are pieces of information that contribute to identification. The last purpose relates to the security of those who intervene in the autopsy. It can occur, and this has occurred, that explosive devices, grenades, for example, that were buried with the body or sharp objects which could be dangerous for the person carrying out the autopsy. Those are the three reasons why, before carrying out an autopsy, we carry out fluoroscopic or X-ray examination. Then you have the description of the injuries that were noted after the external examination and during the autopsy, that is, the dissection of the body. And to make things perfectly clear, the human body is subdivided, the head and neck, the trunk, the upper limbs, and the two lower limbs. And lastly we examine the internal tissue, but very often in this kind of autopsy, given the demonstration relating to putrification, it provides much less information because the tissue has already decomposed and putrefied.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you refer to the section on injuries. We see that there are three boxes there: Probably - and to the right - probably ante mortem; probably post mortem; and cannot tell. That's at the bottom of the page. Can you explain that? We see here it's left blank on this specific ...

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Some injuries might have occurred after death, either because the dead body was damaged, injured, after death, there could be an explosion nearby or injuries related to animal scavengers, or any other origin -- injury that might have occurred during exhumation. And these injuries can be identified by certain characteristics, and they have to be distinguished from injuries that occurred at the time of death or before the time of death. I must say that I really don't like the term "probably ante mortem." I prefer the term peri mortem because if you use ante mortem, that also includes any other previous injuries, any other medical injuries. An old fracture, for example, would be included in the term "ante mortem." I prefer the term per i mortem to refer to injuries that occurred at the point in time of death or just before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could look at page 3 of this exhibit we see that there are a number of injuries that are noted there, but again the boxes that refer to whether the injury was ante mortem or post mortem have not been filled out. Is this normal to not indicate whether the injury is ante mortem or pots mortem, or would this be something that you would expect to find in these type of autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, indeed. I don't know exactly why Professor Vanezis did not check these boxes. I myself did insist that these boxes be checked off when I myself in the year 2000 carried out autopsies with my team. It is difficult to distinguish between ante mortem and post mortem injuries in some cases, that's a fact, but I believe that if there is a difficulty in that case then the forensic specialist should check the last box, that is, "cannot tell."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We saw when we were looking at the first page of this exhibit that the cause of death, according to Professor Vanezis, was multiple gun-shot wounds. What does that tell you with regard to the type of injuries suffered by this person? And I'm referring specifically to the fact -- I'm asking this specifically because these boxes have not been marked.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I believe it was something that he simply omitted to do. The very fact of declaring that the cause of death was multiple gun-shot wounds signifies quite clearly that those wounds were of the category either ante mortem or peri mortem, as I prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we can look at one more page of this report, this is page 8, and this is part of the report which you had explained earlier was the handwritten report that is prepared during the examination. And I would -- just would like to draw your attention to the sentence which refers to: "Modified blood present in right chest cavity." If you can comment on that observation which is contained in this report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I also noted that sentence here, which emphasizes the ante mortem or peri mortem occurrence of these injuries, of the fracture. In a skeleton it's difficult to examine the semiology and determine whether it's ante mortem or post mortem. But when you still have soft tissue, body organs, and viscera, you can, in that case, if you had the laceration of left lung, you had rib fractures, and also the area covered by these ribs, that is, the lung was injured; and if you have blood inside the thorax, it means that there was an injury that bled and that the blood collected in the chest. And this proves that the injury was either ante or peri mortem. And if -- upon examination of the autopsy photographs that you gave to me, numerous pictures showed indeed the presence of modified blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We have spoken very briefly about the cause of death. Could you tell us in -- just in very general terms the criteria that are usually used to establish the cause of death during such autopsies as the one we're looking at right now.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: There are numerous criteria. You take inventory of the wounds and some of these wounds did not cause death, for example, a fractured finger is not going to be a cause of death. We examine the consequences for the body of certain wounds. A multi-fragmented fracture of the skull, a comminuted fracture, will lead to brain damage which cannot be treated, and in that case the cause of death is obvious. If you're talking about chest wounds, if you have a fractured rib on one side and on the other related to a projectile, we know that in anatomical terms the fracture surrounds very major organs, and therefore any such fracture can lead to death. The heart is situated very close to that area and major veins and aorta as well, and that can be a cause of death. Third example, a vertebrae in the neck or in the back, if you -- if, for example, a projectile had shattered a vertebrae, this will damage the bone marrow, which is essential, of course, for a number of the bodily functions and this can be a cause of death. In some cases, it may be necessary to carry out a more detailed examination. For example, if you have a projectile wound of the femur. If the trajectory goes in towards the front, it may hit the femoral artery. This will not cause immediate death, but if there is no care provided then the person can die haemorrhaging or of shock following the injury of this artery which is a very large artery and which is very close to the femur. So, you see, all of these aspects are examined when we analyse the cause of death. We go through all of the wounds that have been discovered during the autopsy, and this is compared with the major functions of the human body and that enables us to determine the most probable cause of death, the most obvious cause of death. When you have multiple projectiles, you will have several potential causes of death, if you have a chest wound, for example, close to the heart and a wound in the skull. Death is something that doesn't necessarily occur immediately. It may take several minutes, and therefore we define priorities, we define a hierarchy of the potential causes of death. And therefore, this analysis includes all of this information which leads to determining the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during the conduct of a forensic examination, who determines the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The forensic pathologist who is in charge of the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: And who is the expert who, in fact, coordinates the team of experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what role, if any, does a forensic anthropologist [Realtime transcript read in error "pathologist"] have when establishing the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The forensic anthropologist, over and beyond the work that he provides during exhumation, he works with the archaeologist during exhumation; but in the morgue the anthropologist, forensic pathologist, works in cooperation with the forensic pathologist. The anthropologist participates in the inventory of the body parts. The -- he will be concentrating on skeletal remains, that is, where the soft tissue has disappeared. He will take stock of the bones, in particular when you have co-mingled bones, we already spoke of the concept of minimum number of individuals. It is the anthropologist who will determine how many individuals were to be found in a particular grave. Secondly, and this is an important function, they contribute to determining the gender if the soft tissue of the genital parts has disappeared, it is anthropological criteria that are used to determine the gender of the body. I mentioned earlier the discriminating value in particular of the pubic bones or the skull that contribute to determining the gender of the body, and that is the anthropologist's function. They also determine the age of the victim. They work with the odontologist because the determination of age is also based on the analysis of the dental structure. The anthropologist will work hand in hand with the pathologist to give an opinion on the cause of death. But the main forensic expert is the forensic pathologist who takes account of the opinions of the other specialists that work with him and takes on the responsibility for drafting the report, for signing the report. It is the forensic pathologist who signs the death certificate and therefore in the eyes of the law, as is the case at national level, it is the forensic pathologist who takes responsibility for determining the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender Exhibit 05005 into evidence. And I see it's time for the break. Just one correction before that -- before we have the break with regard to the transcript: I see page 30, line 1, my question was "What role if any does a forensic anthropologist... " and the transcript reads "pathologist." I would just like to correct that. And I seek to tender the report that we have up on the screen into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a convenient time, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have very little left in direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, we must have a break now, which is for 30 minutes while the tapes are rewound. A Court Officer will assist you during the break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, I had shown the witness Exhibit 05009, and I was just reminded by Ms. Pedersen, I forgot to tender it into evidence, so I seek that that be admitted. It's the report which the witness was commenting on earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01142.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, if we could have Exhibit 05006 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we have another document up on the screen. This is again on autopsy report for the same site, and we see this is case JS001/007B and which indicates under "Cause of Death" a -- gun-shot injuries to the chest and head injury. If we could move to the second page of this exhibit, we see that under heading "A. Description of Remains" there's a sentence that says: "This information most probably refers to body JS001/008." Is this what you were referring to earlier when you indicated that there was a case that you had seen where the identification number has been switched with another -- the remains of another victim?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see here that the victim has been identified as Shefkate Bogujevci, born in 1956, and under the age-range we have a range of 17 to 19. If -- would the reason for this discrepancy between the date of birth and the age-range that's indicated here be the fact that this report actually corresponds to another body which is indicated there under the description field?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this report, it's 05006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01143.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we could now have 05007 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that this report refers to case number JS001/008B, and under cause of death we have gun-shot wound to the head. Now if we turn the page to page 2, and I would just ask you to comment on what -- on the information contained under the "Description of Remains."

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Description of remains, here it states that in addition to the information relating to the position of the body, there was a piece of paper with the name "Nora (Selatin) Bogujevci born in 1984." And this is in contradiction with the age determined by anthropological measures which gives an interval between 44 and 55 years of age. And as the forensic specialist, Professor Vanezis, states, the information on this piece of paper most likely refers to the body JS001/007 whose age corresponds as well as the presence of an earring.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And that was the report that we just saw, Case 007 was the earlier report we just had on the screen; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 05007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01144.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's -- there are a series of other reports that correspond to this site. In the interests of saving time, I do not plan to go through each one of these reports. They follow the same format as the ones we've already seen. Earlier this morning I provided the Registrar with a list of the different exhibit numbers for those reports and the Defence also have a copy. So I would also ask that -- to proceed with these exhibits being assigned exhibit numbers at a later stage by a memo rather than have me read out all the exhibit numbers in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, and the Registrar in due course will notify parties of the numbers assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, at this stage I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Baccard. I am Dragoljub Djordjevic, and I am the Defence counsel for the accused here. I will have some questions for you, and I will try not to refer to the matters that have already been admitted into evidence. My first question for you is the following: When were you engaged by the ICTY, or rather, the OTP of this Tribunal, when did this happen the first time?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Could you specify your question, sir. Are you asking me when I was first hired by the OTP or whether -- when I was hired to draft this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm -- what I would like to hear is when was it the first time that the OTP of this Tribunal actually hired you.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I first served at the OTP in 1999, and I went to Bosnia for a few weeks in Visegrad. I cannot recall exactly what month that was, but you'll find it in my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The report that you've prepared is -- was prepared in accordance with a contract that you entered into with the OTP of this Tribunal in 1999 or later? Because I note that this report is a report from 2001.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, I then had short-term contracts with the OTP, and the review of the documents that were submitted to me and the drafting of the report occurred later, I think it was 2001. But I couldn't tell you which month that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. My next question will be about the team-work of your colleagues, the work of the teams, forensic pathologists and anthropologists, in the period between June up until the end of 1999, which is when this work was done. You were in no way connected with them at the time, and I'm referring to 1999, or were you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I assume you are referring to the teams whose work I reviewed in my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, no, I had no specific contacts with any of them apart from a number of contacts with Commissaire Gaillardon, who in those days was the deputy head of the forensic police department at the French Ministry of Home Affairs, and I had worked with him on the Mont Blanc tunnel disaster investigation. We had both been members of the team trying to identify the bodies and the remains that had -- that were in the tunnel, but that was completely disconnected to what happened in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The work that was done in 1999 by your colleagues from France, Switzerland, the United States, Great Britain, and I see there were also teams from White Russia, Finland, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, did these teams perform the work ad hoc - and I'm referring to June and on wards, 1999 - or was there some kind of coordination between the teams?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe that those teams came together beforehand, before the mission, and were brought together by the OTP of the ICTY in order to give them certain instructions on the basis of the reports that I examined that was not expressed clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To be honest, the interpretation that I received was such that I am not clear on what your answer was. So my question is: Do you have any knowledge as to whether these teams worked in coordination or not? And the first question will be: Do you have any knowledge of that at all?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe that there must have been some coordination, but I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me if I say that you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: According to what Commissaire Gaillardon stated, there was one meeting they had in The Hague before they went to Kosovo on site, but I can't tell you anything else about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From your question [as interpreted] I assume and I conclude that you don't have any knowledge as to whether there was a body in 1999 that coordinated the work of these teams who worked on the forensic expertise of the site that you later speak about and discuss in your report; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My second question: You mentioned a list of some 20 different experts, most of them were forensic pathologists, but there were also anthropologists that participated in the expert work. And what I would like to know is whether you contacted any of these individuals when -- while preparing this report and in connection with the report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, in order to ask for clarifications, that was the case for one team, the French team, that is Professor Lecomte and Dr. Vorhauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose because you come from the same country, you and Professor Lecomte, that you knew the professor from before; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that person. I had met the doctor at conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There were at least six or -- seven or eight teams that worked on autopsies or simply on surveying the sites and so forth. In view of that fact, did you have occasion to speak with the team leaders of each of these teams that actually did the work on site, in connection with the reports that they submitted and that you commented upon?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No. Either it wasn't necessary or for reasons of time there was not enough time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Whether that was necessary or not will be something that I will come back to a little later and with reference to the report that you prepared. What I would like to know now is this: Does your science - and I mean primarily your speciality, in other words, in the most general of terms I'm referring to forensic pathology and medicine - is there a methodology that must be followed when expert reports or autopsies are done on human remains?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, there are main principles of methodology which are universally accepted in scientific circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From your colleagues, forensic pathologists, who have already testified before this Tribunal, I heard that there are different methodologies that can be used and that there were different schools in this respect. Could you briefly just tell us whether that is true? That's one.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. There are consensus, conferences, if you will, that have been organised as regards the way observations should be made in order to carry out an autopsy, recommendations have been made within the European Union, there's also a protocol handed down by the International Academy of Forensic Medicine; and these schools, in fact, have minor differences amongst them. There may be a different approach depending on the origin of the forensic expert, in particular to give you an example, the case of incisions. There are several ways of approaching the dissection of the trunk and the neck and there are certain variations depending on whether you're from Europe or from the UK or the United States, but these are differences that do not call into question the essential aspects. It is a question of habit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is important here is that this does not affect the essential aspects. However, we have a Swiss team here - and you referred to that in particular - then we have a US team and a British team here, as well as Finnish, French, European teams in general. The several observations that you made that deal with different approaches in particular, were these observations made by you of such quality that they may affect the final outcome of the autopsy reports performed on the bodies in view of these forensic experts who come from various parts and who conducted the examinations on site, on various sites?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As I mentioned, generally speaking, at the end of each annex where I presented comments on each report, these comments do not call into question the general conclusions made by the various different reports. Although the approaches were different, the conclusions are valid from a scientific point of view in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When reading your report in the instance, for instance, of Racak or Vata sites, I noticed that you mentioned that there was no identification done, either at Racak or Vata. What was the reason for that? And I couldn't figure that out based on your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I do not have a reference for the English version, but in the B/C/S version it is on page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But in any case what it says there is that there was no identification done at Racak or Vata. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask your permission to be able to refer to a copy of my report which I have in my briefcase because it's very difficult to answer that question without examining the document precisely that has just been referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would seem desirable, Mr. Djordjevic? Yes, Doctor, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please repeat the paragraph that you mentioned in your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Doctor. This is the portion of your report relating to Vata, identification paragraph 1.3.4.2, and then on the next page I noticed that where you discuss Racak it is stated here that: "The identification process was not adhered to in the reports about Racak and Vata." And what I would like to know is: What does that mean, that the identification process was not adhered to?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That does not mean that the identification work was not continued. What this means is that I did not have, in the documents that I was given, the results of the identification process which had been carried out. In particular, the DNA work was not included. That does not mean that it hadn't been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is quite clear, but what it says in your report literally is this, and that's the last sentence before the paragraph entitled "sex ratio," 1.3.4.3, it says: "In addition, the identification process was not adhered to in the reports about Racak and Vata at the time of the autopsies." Do you have any knowledge as to whether the identification process was completed later on for these two sites?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: There is a footnote which states that at the point in time when this report was drafted, according to the information that had been confirmed to me, the percentage of identification of the Racak victims was 100 per cent. But in the documents that I had been given and which referred to the autopsy reports in particular by the Finnish team, at the point in time when that autopsy report was drafted, they did not have that information. However, at the point in time when I drafted my report, we did have that information. However, I did not have access to those documents proving the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You did give a partial answer to my next question when you said that regarding Racak the identification was performed 100 per cent, so I did not really understand this sentence at first, but now it's clearer. I'd only like you to tell me: Do you know who finalised the identification to the degree of 100 per cent, as indicated in the footnote, because the footnote says that the Finnish team did not submit this data, at least not at the time of your report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next and last question about this context is this: Why did you enter this 100 per cent in this rubric? That remains unclear.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, that was because I got that information from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a document confirming that to enable you to put "100 per cent" there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure you received that information from the Office of the Prosecutor, or are you unsure about that as well? Because it's quite seriously illogical; that's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, I must -- I did get this information, information that was sufficiently reliable for me to mention it in my report. Had there been a reason to doubt, I would have said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But you will admit and you'll agree with me that there is a difference, discrepancy, between your claim that the identification was not continued and the assertion that it is now finalised 100 per cent. As far as I know, reports of this kind can be made only on the basis of documented and certain evidence documented by experts, your colleagues, forensic pathologists. So may I conclude and will you agree with me that you in fact did not have the reports of the forensic pathologists who identified these victims at the time when you entered this percentage, 100?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, two things. First of all, I don't -- it's not my recollection that the witness stated that the identification was not continued. I understood him saying quite the opposite earlier up in the transcript. And I believe also that he has already answered this question to the best of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Like Ms. Kravetz, Mr. Djordjevic, I understood the doctor to indicate that while he may not have had the identification results, he understood that it had been conducted. And, for example, in the case of Racak his report specifically states 100 per cent of victims had been identified by the date of his report. So I think that premise of your question is not accurate. And I agree with Ms. Kravetz that the doctor's already answered what you're now asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree the doctor has answered; however, I was trying to refresh the witness's memory relating to the documentation -- in fact, the sentence that I read out, but I will not insist any further. I appreciate what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your report, Witness, you speak of the clothing found on the victims. In some of the reports it is said that some of the victims had military clothing or civilian clothing; in other reports no such distinction is made. Does this discrepancy, this difference, mean that there was no uniform approach at the time when making autopsy reports or is there another explanation that I would like to hear from you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I believe I answered that question by saying that I used the documents and the material that I had received. I quite clearly established a review of what was in these reports, and the fact is that in the reports that I had been given it is sometimes indicated and sometimes not. When it isn't indicated, there is -- there are a number of photographs that allow us to see how the victim was dressed and what the victim was wearing at the time of exhumation, and I quite simply described what I saw on the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You did say this before, but my question was: Can you agree with me that the methodology applied on the ground was not uniform at the time among the teams that provided expertise?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, on that specific issue what I am trying to tell you is that in some reports we had indications and others not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really follow the interpretation, but obviously you did not understand the gist of my question. Would you agree with me that at that time, in 1999, there was no structured methodology and a uniformed method of performing autopsies by pathologists and anthropologists; instead, each team worked as best they saw fit?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: It is true that there are variations in the way the reports are constructed, as I have said in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now I have a question on page 17 in B/C/S, items 1.4, 1.5, in the second paragraph, about Izbica. You say there that on the videotape the corpses look fresh or with the earliest signs of decomposition. Other bodies show signs of advanced decomposition. Now, this video recording was made by Dr. Liri Loshi. I'm interested in the recordings, the video footage, of those corpses in the field. Did you really use the word that I heard in interpretation, "fresh" corpses or corpses that were exhumed? Because the two don't go together. If they were fresh, they couldn't have been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: So what's your question exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question, did this video recording show, as you put it, as I heard in interpretation, the corpses seem fresh or with some signs of beginning putrefaction? Were these bodies indeed exhumed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I think there are two elements in the video. I'm -- I can't recall exactly, but I think I'm referring to two phases in the video. In one of the -- in the first part there are fresh bodies or only initial signs of decomposing, and then there's another part in which there are bodies that have been exhumed apparently two months after they were first buried, and are therefore in an advanced state of decomposing. I must say, I can't quite remember the video. We should refer to it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What we established so far in these proceedings is that Dr. Liri Loshi made that recording just a day or two after these people had lost their lives, but that's why I'm asking you. I did not see, although I watched the videotape, I did not see any bodies that had been exhumed and in an advanced state of putrefaction. That's why I'm asking you: Why did you mention this in your report? What is this assertion based on? Can you look up your documentation because it would be really important for me to know.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: If we're looking at the second paragraph of item 1.4.5 where it starts: "Then these victims appear to be exhumed approximately two months after the burial in an advanced state of putrefaction." I think it refers to the moment when the bodies were exhumed and therefore made available to the French forensic team. But please remember, this happened a few years ago. I've seen many other videos and been an expert in many other cases since then, and I can't remember exactly that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
