utterances.text: It's obvious that you can't recall this and even more confusion is introduced in your report by the sentence in the same paragraph that begins with the words: "It seems that the cause of death was difficult to establish judging by the fact that it was impossible to perform an external examination in autopsies because of the disappearance of the bodies." My question in relation to this --

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Exactly, so it makes sense. There's no contradiction in what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have before you the report of your colleagues from France on these autopsies? Did they perform a complete autopsy, including an external examination of the bodies? Because you say here that there was a need to work on video images taking -- without respect of the standards of scientific photography. What did they work on? Did they have any direct contact with the bodies? What can we conclude from your report? It sounds a bit equivocal on that.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I examined indeed the reports that were drafted by the French teams. There was a crime scene report and a photography album entitled Crime Scene Investigation carried out by Commissaire Gaillardon and his team. And I also examined what was titled Autopsy Report by Professor Vorhauer and Lecomte, as well as the video that was given to me. As regards the human remains that the French team examined, these were small body parts, human body parts, there were five bone fragments, in particular skull bones and forearm bones and also skin fragments that were found inside of socks and 21 tufts of hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So we may conclude that your colleagues were not, in fact, able to perform complete autopsies on the alleged minimum of 27 bodies; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and this has been stated on several occasions in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding this video recording, you said in your report that it was a video that was not made by a professional. It was made by one of your colleagues, a pathologist. What did you mean when you said that it was an amateur video? It was, after all, a doctor who made it.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Because these images were not carried out in -- with forensic purposes in mind. As I explained earlier this morning, the bodies are lined up, side by side. They were not mobilised in such a way to show not only the side that is visible but the other side on which the body is lying. The body has been covered with blankets, and therefore only certain portions of the anatomy can be seen on the video. In addition, the video is shot from a certain distance, and therefore the image is not as clear as it would be had you done a professional forensic video. And that's why I stated that this video did not correspond to the professional criteria. What I meant was forensic criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'd like to ask you now to try to remove a contradiction, what I believe is a contradiction, in your report. And that takes us back to the bodies seen allegedly on this video footage that were in advanced state of putrefaction. It is supposed that they were exhumed after lying in the ground for two months. This is not at all consistent with the claim that your colleagues did not have access to actual remains from the grave in Izbica. They only had access to body parts.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I believe there's a misunderstanding. I remember exactly how that sentence was drafted in my report. I was told that those bodies had been exhumed after two months. The video includes pictures which are referred to in my report, that is, bodies that have very few or no signs of decomposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Here we have a specific explanation and thank you for that. My next question would have to do with the annexes to your report. They begin with Racak. All I want to know is: Are you familiar with the assertions of your colleague, Dr. Helena Ranta of Finland made several years after the forensic expertise provided by a very broad Finnish team of experts? Can you comment if you are familiar?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Dr. Helena Ranta is from Finland indeed. She's not Swedish; she's Finnish. She has written a number of publications, but I'm not familiar with her statements. I have no knowledge of her statements as regards this case in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking of the differences and contradictions between the reports of the Finnish expert team on the one hand and the Yugoslav and Byelorussian teams on the other hand. Can you just give me a general answer, because you named these differences and discrepancies in your report, but can you give us a general comment as an expert on these discrepancies between the Yugoslav and Byelorussian teams on one hand and the Finnish expertise from the point of view of principle.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As regards these discrepancies, some are minor, related essentially to terminology matters; others may be of greater importance, in particular the number of shots or the number of projectiles, or perhaps the distance from which the shot occurred. You can examine these discrepancies one by one, but generally speaking I did list the discrepancies that I discovered between the two reports. The two teams had access to the same corpses at -- either at different points in time or at the same point in time and it was interesting to see how this was described in each of their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding annex number 2 which is attachment number 3 -- sorry, regarding another one of the annexes, annex number 3 regarding Bela Crkva and Annex 4 concerning Padaliste as well as Izbica, I would have this question: In view of the gravity of discrepancies and inconsistencies you found, did you contact any of the members of these teams who provided expertise on the spot to deal with these inconsistencies in your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: These discrepancies are not all major, they're not all important. In some cases these are minor differences; in other cases they're of a greater importance. To answer your question, I had time constraints such that I was not able to go through such a large volume of documents and to make contact with each of the expert teams that had drafted the reports, each from a different country. Therefore, as I explained, this was the case only for the French team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: More than once today you mentioned that you did not have enough time at your disposal. How much time did you really have for making this report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Until the beginning of the Milosevic trial. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is not a very precise answer, but it's certain that you did not have enough time. If you had had enough time, what more should have been done to make your report more precise and to remove all the in -- unclarities?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As regards some of the more important discrepancies, it would have been preferable to be able to contact the authors of those reports. The matter was discussed at the time with the person in charge of investigations, and this was not followed up on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at your report on Padaliste. You say in item 2: "In seems that in all cases the date of death was stated incorrectly, the second half of May, 1999, although it did happen sometime in May 1999." How do you know, for instance, that it's not May but March?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Could you please give me a page number that you're quoting from?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's annex -- just a second. Annex 4, Padaliste, beyond page 100 certainly in English and in French because I can see that from the B/C/S version. Annex 4, Padaliste, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, if I state it it's quite simply because it appeared somewhere else in a more reliable fashion in one of the documents that had been given over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now let's take a look at paragraph 3. It says: "There is no precision concerning used methodology." And then you say: "It does not seem there was practice radiographic and/or fluoroscopic examination nor samples taken." The phrase that you use, "seem," is this your assumption or can you actually ascertain that this was actually the case?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: There was no mention of radiographic exams or of samples being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is claimed that there were at least 54 victims found on this site. You will agree with me that this is a large number. This analysis was performed by a British team. Does this bring into question the competence of this team in view of what you state here, in other words, there was no radiographic or fluoroscopic examination done nor samples taken. There is no certain data as to the calibre of the weapons and so on and so forth. Let's not go into the details of your report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The competence of the British team.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: There is no reason why we should call into question the competence of the British team because there was no specific information relating to X-rays. X-rays cannot in any way replace the quality of a human examination and dissection when projectiles are found in a human body; you have it whether there was or wasn't an X-ray previously. The only difference is that if there was no X-rays, maybe other projectiles were overlooked. This being said, the conclusions of the positive evidence of the presence of projectiles is valid and is -- remains valid and there's no reason to call into question the competence of these experts. You must remember also that the conditions in which these examinations were conducted are not those that you find in the morgues and mortuaries of developed countries where you have a specific time-frame, electricity, water-supplies. No. Remember that we were working in an emergency situation. And similar to what you have in war medicine or war surgery, with triage on the field, well you have exactly the same here. Once the safety of the teams has been assured and guaranteed, these teams intervene, but the infrastructure and equipment they had was not -- was maybe not optimal. In my view, there is no reason to be upset by the fact that there was no mention of X-rays in the report. Again, to conduct X-rays you have to have the right X-ray machines, to be able to supply -- transport the machine, have electricity supplies, constant electricity supply, protect the personnel and the staff against ionising radiation. You therefore need sandbags or lead protection. You need to protect the thyroids of the people. So this is something you absolutely require to conduct X-rays. There is no reason, again, why we should call into question the competence of these experts, these well-renowned experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Why are samples taken? You mention the word "shocking," which I did not use. But why are samples taken, and why did you say that samples were not taken on this case. What is the meaning of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Again, what I'm saying is that there is no mention in the report that samples had been taken. The reason why biological samples are taken are varied. One of the purposes of such biological samples is to have an anthropological one. We may want, for instance, to look at specific bones that will help us identify the age and gender of the victim. For instance, the front of the fourth rib or the pelvic bone that can then be interpreted - and indeed there are charts and tables that we can review them against, but to do so you therefore have to prepare things. You need to remove the cartilage, remove the soft tissue, and that is something that cannot be done at the time of the autopsy. It must be done later on. There are other samples, other biological samples, that can be taken, bones or teeth, that are examined from a genetic point of view, to find the DNA and compare it with reference DNA, either the DNA of the victim itself or of relatives of the victim. In terms of practices on crime scenes and war scenes, this is -- these are the samples that are usually taken, over and beyond the usual samples that might be taken in other circumstances, for instance, samples to test on the toxicology, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. It is much clearer now. Now, you mention the very end of the conflict in Kosovo and -- which was a time when your colleagues arrived in Kosovo and what the conditions were then. Do you actually have real information as to what the conditions were in fact for conducting investigations in Kosovo at the time in -- we're discussing here?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I have information on the place where the autopsies were carried out, and that is included in my report. I have information on the dates at which these autopsies were carried out. And when I referred to the venue where these autopsies were carried out, I state whether it was a mortuary or whether it was just a makeshift mortuary, with improvised equipment, just a plank of wood on -- standing on chairs maybe, and this is supported by evidence -- by photographic evidence. And indeed, you can see that these are sub-standard conditions in which to conduct autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Did such conditions have essential effects on the final findings of the examination and autopsies performed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I think it did play a role, yes, I think it played a role. How much of a role is another question. Look at the possibility of exhuming a body that was buried directly in contact with the soil, therefore a body that started decomposing. There was a transformation of the body fluids, an intermingling of soil, of minerals, of plants, and no access to water to clean, for instance, the skin of the body. If you have a body that has already been damaged where there is lesions, when worms and maggots have started doing their work, it will be increasingly difficult, exceedingly difficult, indeed to identify the smaller lesions that you could have identified had you been able to wash the body. But the major wounds, the major lesions, the ones that actually cause death, quite simply because they are big, visible, and have an impact on vital organs, will be visible and identifiable. So the answer is yes, but it has no impact on the main lesions and the conclusions of the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What you've just said now, in that respect experts would pronounce their views on the manner in which the lesions or wounds were afflicted. They analysed the distance from which a shot was fired that caused the death of an individual. They analysed the conditions under all of this happened. Could you, please, briefly tell us, in various degrees of putrefaction of a body, to what extent is it possible to establish all those things under the conditions that prevailed at the time when your colleagues performed these analyses and examinations on site.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I expect you are referring to the distance at which the shot was fired. It is true that the determination of the distance of the shot -- of firing the shot is much more difficult to establish on a decomposed body. As you know, the distance is established by taking into account a number of criteria. When there are multiple projectiles, you look at the way in which the projectiles are scattered; but when there's a single projectile, it is true that you look at the dust and the way it is scattered across the skin and clothes. Now, if you have putrefied teguments, it becomes much more difficult to identify these areas on the body where small debris and particles have been imprinted in the body. And when indeed there has been the beginnings of decomposing after burial, it makes it more difficult. As for the analysis of clothing, it is true that clothes bear these indications slightly longer. On -- when you have a shot fired at a very short range, there will be an indication on the bones that are just below the skin. There will be some kind of an imprint on the bone, an imprint that you will not find these prints on the skin if -- if it is at such a close range that the gun is standing on the bone, standing on the skull, for instance, the imprints will be on the bone and not on the skin. There are also other indications similar to that. So, yes, it is much more difficult to identify the distance at which the shot was made, but there are usually enough indications for the expert to come to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this exhaustive answer. It will be of use to all of us I'm sure. Now, discussing the expertise, which is not very common, and that you have which is medical ballistics, you mentioned the shots fired from the immediate distance, relative distance - and I understand what a greater distance means. But what we haven't heard so far in any of your testimonies was a distinction between absolute vicinity and relative vicinity of shot fired. Could you just briefly explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, when a shot is fired we tend to distinguish -- when we discuss wound ballistics, we're talking about a shot from a very close distance on contact, in other words, the gun is right on the skin or -- then you have other shots a few centimetres from the body, and then you have a third category, a longer range. And I mentioned the criteria a moment ago that is the imprint of the gunpowder and the -- the tattoo as I call it. There are a range of factors which will have an effect on the size of this imprint on the skin, that is, the length of the gun; various equipment used, a silencer, for example, to silence the noise will have an impact; the use of a Magnum, for example, will leave more powder traces at a longer distance than others. So a lot depends -- there are a number of factors that come into play related to the weapon itself and also the ammunition used. There is also the possibility of some sort of a screen, some sort of object, in between the gun and the victim which will also modify the impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, in a physical sense what does it mean point-blank or absolute vicinity; and close-range or relative vicinity? Is there any measurable criteria or is this just a general distinction?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: You mean in terms of distance in centimetres?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What is "close-range"? I understand what point-blank is. I understand that to mean that the weapon -- the muzzle of the weapon is actually next to the body of the -- or in contact with the body of the victim, but what do you mean by close range or relative distance?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, the term "relative distance" is not used in ballistics. We talk about short range, close range, but the word "relative" is not used. I'm not familiar with that term. I don't know if I've answered your question or perhaps you need additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have given a full answer, because I have a translation here and this is a term that was probably chosen by the translators, "relative vicinity," but now after your explanation it's all clear and I thank you for your reply. Now, my next question will be this and it will have to do with Annex 8, I believe, the Dubrava site. The investigation there was performed by your colleagues from Spain, Spanish pathologists, and at the very beginning in the general section of your comments you say that: "One should take with some reservation the distinction made between..." Have you found this, Professor? That there should be a distinction made between small and large shrapnel which can distinguish between hand-grenades and aerial bombs. Could you just explain this in some more detail in view of your specialities. In other words, aerial bombs as opposed to -- and the distinctions between aerial bombs and hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not really because lesional ballistics deals with projectiles, that is, ballistic studies, the movement of a projectile in the air, but does not deal with explosives. The only thing I wanted to mention in this report was that I, myself, did not accept the distinction that had been made by my Spanish colleagues between small shrapnel and large shrapnel for the simple reason that the size itself of the shrapnel is only one factor amongst many, which enables you to determine the origin of the explosive device. When an explosion occurs, there is the generation of numerous different shrapnels of various sizes, and it's not just the size but also the thickness and the nature of the shrapnel which enables an expert to determine whether it's a hand-grenade, a rocket. It's not the size itself. It's the size plus a number of other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, your claim that it seems better to have some reservations on this distinction, you will agree with me that this means that there is no one safe-proof method in order to determine what a person was injured by and what type of projectile or fragment caused the injury?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, I'm -- I beg your pardon. I don't accept that statement. Each expert must limit himself to his own specialty. A forensic pathologist must limit himself to those matters, a ballistics expert to those matters, et cetera. And it is up to the ballistics expert to examine the shrapnel, and it is only the conclusions drawn from that laboratory that will enable you to determine the actual origin of this or that shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm trying to show here, where you say that it seems better to take this with some reservation. So this would mean that -- you will agree with me that this means that each expert should perform their own part of the job. For instance, you said that a ballistics expert should determine what type of projectile and so on. Is that what you meant by what you said?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The forensic pathologist, if he or she has knowledge of another field of expertise must nonetheless be very cautious and limit his findings to certain aspects and not make comments outside of his or her field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This same appendix, Appendix 8, under item 2 entitled "Individual Remarks" mentions case number 9. And you say that the cause of death there in the case that it's suicide but it seems to be an error because the victim sustained two gun-shot wounds in the right anterior lateral part of the chest. Could you tell us briefly if you can recall this case; and if not, we won't dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: In the report, I noted that indeed for this case the cause of death was given as suicide. This is very unusual in the series of reports that I examined, and therefore I thought that it was a mistake given that the victim had sustained two gun-shot wounds in a zone which is unusual in cases of suicide. And therefore, I thought that it might have been a mistake in interpretation or simply a mistake in the drafting of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any description - and I haven't seen it and that's why I want to ask you - why is the word "suicide" mentioned at all? I see that you were surprised by it too, and I am surprised by it as well. Why is the word "suicide" used here at all? Was there some additional information that had nothing to do with the expertise and the examinations? Do you recall anything that could explain this?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, I'm very sorry. I don't remember precisely that aspect of the report. I don't know if we can get a copy easily. If the report is available, perhaps I can give you a better answer. But with the information that I have here, I can't give you a better answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to move to a topic that will take our full focus, and so I propose that we take a break now so that I can deal with that topic in one go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the break a few minutes early and resume at five minutes before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in -- Your Honour, I just wanted to indicate that I had a discussion with my learned colleague concerning the list of exhibits that I proposed to tender as underlying materials to the report, and I understand that Mr. Djordjevic now does not object to any of those documents. So I will ask that all of that list be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. They will be the subject of notification in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Baccard, I will continue with the questions that the Defence believes to be important. Regarding all these reports, I'd be interested to know whether within any report by any team if you noticed that they had used crime investigation documentation prepared by the Yugoslav authorities regarding the scenes of crime where forensic expertise was done and autopsies.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I do not think I have made any mention and -- or reference to documents coming from Yugoslavia -- or rather, I think there might have been some relating to Racak. I seem to remember that Yugoslav pathologists with the assistance of Byelorussian pathologists wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Swiss team did the Muslim cemetery in Kacanik and worked in Kotlina and I believe also in another location Stagovo. Did Swiss experts perform only the external examination or did a complete identification because they noted the location, the origin, and types of wounds and injuries, and did they try to establish whether the injuries occurred before death or after death and which weapon was used?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understood your question, sir. You seem to want to ask me about the way in which the Swiss team operated in Kotlina and Dubrava; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, let me turn to my papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me correct myself, Dubrava is actually not one of them. It's Kacanik, Kotlina, and Stagovo, that's where the Swiss team worked.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Now, as concerns Kotlina, the team was a joint team under Dr. Markwalder and Dr. Wyler from the Swiss disaster victim identification team. These autopsies were conducted at the Kacanik cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I must apologise, but I have to review these notes given the time that has passed since these events and since I wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll wait.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: What was the other case you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There are another two cases. One is Kotlina, Kacanik, and I believe Stagovo. Kacanik, Kotlina, and Stagovo.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I think what you're referring to comes up as Dubrava and in brackets Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Dubrava was done by the Spaniards, if I'm not mistaken, Dubrava prison and Dubrava cemetery.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I have it here, Dubrava, Kacanik case, and there are reports by Dr. Markwalder and Wyler who were both members of the Swiss forensic pathology teams dealing with Swiss disaster victim identification. And in Stagovo I have it again that it's Drs. Markwalder and Wyler.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that's what we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: What we have here are autopsies. Can you remind me what your question was, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Would it be fair to say that they performed only an external examination of the bodies and their autopsy reports are very terse, without localisation of wounds, without establishing entry/exit wounds, without determining whether the injuries occurred before or after death, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I had them as being autopsy reports and not external examinations. Let me turn to the annexes, maybe, if you'd be kind enough to tell me which annexes we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, no, because I thought you would remember that because I see the documentation of the Swiss team is very terse. The reports are incomplete and very superficial. And I think it's true what I'm saying, that there was only an external examination of the body and this autopsy report prepared by Dr. Markwalder had no localisation of the wounds, no determination of what fire-arm was used, what projectile, and whether the wound was inflicted before or after death. That's my conclusion at least. It's -- I'd like to hear if you agree or not.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, I would like to be able to refer to a specific page of the report, if you could assist me. You're saying that there is no specific reference to points of entry and points of exit. What case specifically are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Because there are general remarks concerning the work of the Swiss teams without mention of any specifics, but I thought I could elicit some more comment from you. It's not in the annexes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... not in the appendix, it probably means that there were no specific comments I felt I had to make about the methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said. The autopsy report is very terse, no localisation of wounds, no determination of the type of gun. That's what I meant, if you remember something that could be helpful. Now, regarding Kotlina and those wells, the persons whose bodies were found inside the wells, do we know their age? Between 17 and 47? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: We are talking about 2.8 in my report, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I identified the fact that we were talking about the 21-30 years old age bracket that was, in fact, most present and most represented in the list of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did the forensic reports describe the clothing of these victims? I don't see that from your report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I can't remember that, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There are quite a few idiosyncrasies here that I found in other reports as well regarding these wells; however, on the well-preserved parts of the bodies of these victims pulled out from the wells, those who performed the autopsy described 26 gun-shot wounds. How could we explain that the bodies were hit by 14 projectiles more than casings found? And you say in your report that a total of 12 casings were found around the wells. And how come there is such a discrepancy between the gun-shot wounds and the number of casings found in the vicinity of the wells? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt, but I would kindly ask my learned colleague when he's citing from the report if he could give more precise references. I for one am having a bit of difficulty finding the passages that he's just referred to in his last question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you help us there, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to provide a reference. I found it in the reports related to Kotlina. And the esteemed doctor was surely familiar with them. These reports describe the work of the Swiss team precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not stated in Dr. Baccard's report, but that's precisely why I'm asking that it's not stated specifically and there are certain inconsistencies, that documentation prepared by the Swiss team, and that the doctor studied is not specifically mentioned in his expert report. But there are a few inconsistencies I wanted to point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what it is you are referring to other than the report of the doctor so that we can follow the point that you are making? Is it that you have studied the actual original reports prepared by the Swiss team; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely the report I am referring to. And the question that I had started to ask derived from the fact that I looked at these reports together with an expert that I engaged for our Defence team, also a forensic pathologist, and I looked with him at these reports signed by Dr. Christoph Markwalder, the head of the Swiss team, and we noticed those inconsistencies that I'm asking the witness about. Unfortunately I don't have the reference handy. I just thought that the doctor was very familiar with this report from his own work. If he's not, I can't give him the reference right now and we'll have to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard may have great difficulty remembering the content of the actual reports which are not before him at the moment. He has only his own comments, and they contain nothing of what you're referring to. Are you in a position to give us the e-court numbers of the original reports of the Swiss team to which you refer?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's 65 ter 371, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's only Dubrava. However, regarding other locations, I don't have the 65 ter number. And those other locations are Kotlina and Stagovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you will have to be very particular in reminding the doctor of the matters to which you refer, and you will have to hope then that he is able to remember something of what you're speaking about, or else it is likely that the doctor won't be able to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. Then I will ask the doctor if he remembers certain parts of this report; if not, I won't be asking about the wells anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you remember there were two wells there, if you remember the report of the Swiss team, there were wells with bodies inside?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I had no specific recollection of this, but you will see that on page 48 of my report, paragraph 2.8.2, I see here that in brackets after they mention "crime scene 21-1," I indicated that we were referring to the "upper and lower wells." This would suggest that, yes, they were two wells, one slightly higher than the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. And the reports further describe that the altitude between the two wells was around 9 metres. Do you remember that the bodies inside the wells were covered by earth, by soil? For instance, in the upper well at the minimum depth of 7.2 metres and the maximum depth of 9.3 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're going to get into this level of detail with regard to that report, I think in fairness to the witness he should be allowed to at least review it or have it up on the screen. I believe the 65 ter number of the Kotlina report is 00361 if that's the report that my learned colleague is citing to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. You're questioning about Kotlina at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct, the two wells. If we can see 65 ter 361. That's not it. That's the Austrian team. How about -- no, no, that's not it. It's the Austrian report. Can we see page 2, Kotlina, all right. Page 9, please. Do we have an English version? Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this report, Doctor? You saw the first page a moment ago. I'm asking this because it seems to me you did not mention that the Austrian colleagues did this part of the work. That's how the whole confusion occurred.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, if you read my report carefully at 2.8.1 I do say here that this report is based on the report written up by the Austrian crime scene group number 2. Now, I must say I cannot remember now whether the report I'm referring to in my report is the report that is up on the screen, but I do remember that this report existed, and I assume that this Austrian report included the report of the Swiss pathologists, but I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about the report of this Austrian team of forensic pathologists regarding this particular incident and the well. There is reference here to two wells with the victims thrown inside, and it says the minimum depth was 7.2 metres and the maximum depth was 9.3 metres in the upper well. And in the lower well the minimum depth was 5.8 and the maximum 9.7 metres. Bearing in mind what the Austrian experts underlined, namely, the minimal number of casings found around the wells and a very small layer of earth inside the well, can we conclude that the blast wounds occurred outside of the well, that the bodies were in fact found in other locations, dragged to the wells, and thrown inside, or do you believe that the people were actually killed while standing inside the well? What is your conclusion based on the report of this Austrian team?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I would not attempt to draw any conclusions at all at this point. I would like to recall that my report was based essentially on the autopsy reports carried out by my colleagues, and I do not have sufficient recollection at this point in time of the events to draw any conclusions on the basis of what I have here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then I have to ask you a general question. Have you studied the Austrian team's report in this case at all?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The report that I have referred to is the report that I have entitled "Report of the Austrian Crime Scene Group 2." I do not know here today what exactly was the composition of that crime scene group. I was asked to study the forensic aspects and not to examine the crime scene aspects as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then let me ask you this: Things being so, did the Swiss team take into account those parts of the Austrian report that they deemed indispensable to making a complete report? Did these two teams cooperate in any way?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not present when the examination took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's talk about Cirez, the French forensic mission, summer 1999. You said you spoke with your colleague, the professor who headed the French team. Did you discuss this locality, Cirez?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I believe the answer is yes. Let me check. Cirez. Could you give me the reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, doctor, again there were wells in which female bodies were found and it was suspected that the two women had been sexually abused before death.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Let me correct my previous answer. The answer was: No, I was not able to discuss with Professor Lecomte and Vorhauer for the reason that that site was not included in the list of sites that I had been asked to examine by the OTP. It was only afterwards when I testified for the first time in the Milosevic case that I was asked to examine the reports that had been drafted by the French team and to draft an addendum to my own report. That means that it was after the beginning of the trial and I had not had the opportunity to discuss with my colleagues forensic specialists Lecomte and Vorhauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, we can agree that you're referring to the addendum that you compiled as a synthetic reported dated the 31st of January, 2002?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The date that I have is May 23rd, 2002, which was one of the days that I testified in the Slobodan Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And you did that as far as I can recall at the request of my learned colleague Dirk Ryneveld in relation to an excavation of eight bodies from three wells in the Cirez village; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Dirk Ryneveld, I can see in the addendum that I examined the documents on May 22nd/23rd, 2002. And indeed there were three wells with the reference SIP1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We just need to correct an inconsistency. Your report says the forensic findings were the following. You said about age between 18 and 60 -- yes, well, I can see it now, but it was not at the very beginning but in the middle of this text. Now my next question has to do with the stay in Vode for two and a half months. Now, do you know what kind of methodology was used to establish how long the bodies had been under water. Is there a method, whereby one can determine exactly how long a body - a reliable method - how long a body had been in water?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: There are no scientific criteria which makes it possible to estimate in a precise fashion. Findings can be drawn on the basis of the compatibility of the overall aspect of the bodies, its state of conservation, and the date at a given point in time. But we have to be very prudent as regards these matters. It is not possible to make a mathematical -- mathematically precise estimate in this type of situation where the body has been in water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The estimation given here, the two and a half months, that can be found in your addendum and we can see that this was the finding of your colleagues Dominique and Dr. Walter -- Markwalder. Now, does this mean that this assessment should be taken with some reservations and that this means that those bodies could have been immersed under water longer or for a shorter period before they were pulled out of the well?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, no. The way my report is drafted is very clear and states that the date indicates maceration and putrefaction which is compatible of a stay in the water of two months. I said compatible with -- consistent with two months and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking this is that I understood that there is no reliable way to determine how long exactly a body had been immersed. Are you trying to tell me that this can be established in general terms based on the experience that the forensic expert has in this type of work? I'm not clear on this because a few moments ago you said there was no reliable method for determining this, or perhaps I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: No, I believe you've understood. What I said was that there was not a scientific method making it possible to determine on the basis of reliable and mathematically rigorous criteria which would determine the time of immersion in water, but the forensic pathologist is seeing the signs of putrefaction can consider that that is consistent with a particular duration of immersion. There's a big difference between stating a precise date and saying that a set of signs are consistent with a duration of immersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If a body was immersed for two and a half months, what is the method to establish the cause of death in that person? In other words, you understand what my question is referring to. It's referring to how it is that it can be established that a person had actually drowned and not been killed or lost its life before being thrown into a well. What is the method to establish that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The corpse is examined externally and then an autopsy is carried out. The traumatic injury sustained will be modified by immersion in water but will remain in varying degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, if I can ask you even more precisely, is it possible based on autopsy alone to determine that a body, which had been immersed in water for over two months, the cause of death, and whether the cause was drowning, and what are those indicators that could point to that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As I stated in my report, I do not know what the French forensic pathologists based themselves to draw on their -- to other conclusions regarding the cause of death. I don't know whether they examined the anatomy, the pathology, the toxicology such as the amount of strontium, the presence of diatoma which are microscopic cells. None of this information is included in my colleague's report. Therefore, I simply indicated that on the basis of what was stated in their report they, on the basis of the macroscopic findings, those findings were consistent with the diagnosis of drowning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that in fact you have no information as to how your colleagues determined that the cause of death was drowning?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The -- that the data did not enable me to examine those reports in order to check whether or not the findings they present are valid or not, that data was not included in their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question has to do with what we discussed before the break, namely, do you know under what conditions the French team, or rather, your colleagues, Dr. Dominique Lecomte and Dr. Walter Vorhauer, under what conditions did they work, and where did these autopsies occur, where were they conducted? I'm not familiar and I'm not sure about Cirez specifically. And I assume because Cirez was discussed in an addendum that it is an exception.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: In my addendum, I did not indicate what the material conditions under which my French -- the French colleagues worked. I indicated that the team carried out exhumations and recovery and autopsy on the site of Cirez on July 2nd and 3rd, 1999. I don't see any additional information which would enable me to answer your question regarding the actual material conditions at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, after a body has been in water for over two months, is it possible to distinguish from the body itself the changes that were the result of putrefaction and the blood-stains; and if so, on the basis of what can you determine what is in fact --

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Indeed, there are putrefaction transudates and these putrefaction transudates can be found in various cavities of the body. You can also have blood in other areas trapped in tissue. Therefore, you have to differentiate in terms of diagnosis between traumatic lesions which causes the passage of blood into the tissue, haematomas, for example, and other aspects which could lead to confusion which are related to false putrefaction ecchymosis. That is part of the diagnosis that is carried out by the expert. He must differentiate between these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in determining the difference between the fluid created by putrefaction and blood, my understanding was that you need to use certain special chemical compounds in order to determine that. Was that possible under the conditions that prevailed in Kosovo, and especially where we have a body which had spent over two months under water; or is this whole endeavour impossible?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: As I've stated, I do not have any information about the actual material conditions of how those autopsies were carried out. In this particular case, I would simply like to say that Professor Dominique Lecomte and -- who is in charge of the Paris Forensic Laboratory, she is an expert approved by the French Cour de cassation. The same applies to Dr. Vorhauer. They both have extensive experience in autopsies, including individuals who died by drowning. And therefore I would tend to trust them as regards their forensic examinations of individuals in such a situation, in particular if they choose this particular diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this then and that will be my last question for today and I will not be very long tomorrow either. So let's try and find an answer that could resolve this matter. If a body has been under water, let's say, for two and a half months, is it possible to determine with certainty whether the liquid is a blood-stain, in view of the fact that in contact with water blood very quickly haemolysis, or rather, decays? So that would be my question. Perhaps we can get the answer now, regardless of under what conditions your colleagues conducted this investigation.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I cannot give you a general response to your question. Each case is different and these cases have to be examined on a case-by-case basis. What I can say is that over and beyond the haematomas and the ecchymosis there are certain signs on the skin which are not the result of putrefaction, and there is no confusion in that case. Therefore, I would tend to consider that someone who has lengthy professional experience and scholarly experience as the colleagues that I mentioned are in an excellent position to make a decision as regards this type of lesion in spite of the potential traps that I emphasized and that other experts have mentioned regarding the interference of immersion in water and the maceration that's caused by that, putrefaction, the deterioration of tissue that is involved in all of this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Our time is up for today by over two minutes, so I will have to complete my cross-examination for today. And I think that it won't take us very long tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have -- I'm done with this portion of my cross-examination for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. As you've gathered, Doctor, we must finish now. We continue tomorrow. The court officer will give you specific guidance during the break. We look forward to finishing your evidence relatively early in the hearing tomorrow, which commences at 2.15. Thank you.
